extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and practitioners seeking an overview of U.S. First Amendment/freedom-of-speech doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive overview of legal standards, categories, tests, and doctrines the U.S. courts use to evaluate restrictions on speech under the First Amendment. Includes case-law examples and guidance on when speech may be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment baseline: government restriction prohibition and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment prevents government restrictions on speech; when a speech restriction is challenged in court, it is presumed invalid and the government bears the burden of convincing the court that the restriction is constitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom of speech protects free and public expression of opinions without government censorship, interference, or restraint. Protections apply to state and local governments through incorporation. The protection extends to the right to receive information and prohibits most government distinctions between speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-based restrictions — strict scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Content-based restrictions 'are presumptively unconstitutional regardless of the government's benign motive, content-neutral justification, or lack of animus toward the ideas contained in the regulated speech.' Such restrictions must pass strict scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content-based restrictions can discriminate by subject matter or viewpoint; viewpoint discrimination faces the highest level of scrutiny and is usually overturned unless falling within narrow exceptions. Courts look to whether the regulation targets specific messages or viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint discrimination prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: A policy that permits some viewpoints but bans others constitutes viewpoint discrimination and is usually invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a government official who permits opponents of abortion to speak on government property but bans proponents of abortion is engaging in viewpoint discrimination (cited Snyder v. Phelps example). Viewpoint-discriminatory rules face the toughest review and are typically struck down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner restrictions — four requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Time, place, and manner (TPM) restrictions must: be content neutral; be narrowly tailored; serve a significant governmental interest; and leave open ample alternative channels for communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TPM regulations are subject to intermediate scrutiny. They regulate when, where, or how expression occurs without targeting content. 'Ample alternative channels' need not be the speaker's first choice, the same medium, nor reach the same audience (e.g., written rather than vocal). Cases: Grayned v. Rockford; Heffron v. ISC; Cox v. New Hampshire.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Brien test for content-neutral regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A content-neutral regulation is sufficiently justified if: (1) it is within the constitutional power of the Government; (2) it furthers an important or substantial governmental interest; (3) the governmental interest is unrelated to the suppression of free expression; and (4) the incidental restriction on alleged First Amendment freedoms is not greater than is essential to the furtherance of that interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates from United States v. O'Brien (1968). Applied to determine whether a regulation that incidentally burdens speech is constitutionally permissible. Emphasizes unrelatedness of the governmental interest to suppression of expression and narrow tailoring of the incidental burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public forum doctrine — forum classification rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court recognizes three forum types: traditional public forums, designated forums, and nonpublic forums, each with different levels of speech protection and permissible restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional public forums (parks, sidewalks) have the strongest First Amendment protection though TPM rules still apply. Designated forums are government properties opened for public expression and may be limited to certain groups or subjects so long as rules are consistent. Nonpublic forums (airport terminals, internal mail) may be more heavily restricted; restrictions must be reasonable and viewpoint neutral and aligned with the forum's purpose. Cases: Perry, Hazelwood, Widmar, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Government attempts to restrain speech before it is spoken (prior restraint) are disfavored; the government must show that punishment after the fact is not a sufficient remedy and that allowing the speech would 'surely result in direct, immediate, and irreparable damage' (New York Times Co. v. United States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Near v. Minnesota established general prohibition against prior restraints. Prior restraints are rarely permitted; exceptions are narrow. Example: temporary restraining orders against distribution have been subject to challenge and dissolution on hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity — Miller test
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscenity is unprotected speech as determined by the Miller test: speech is obscene if it (1) appeals to the prurient interest (by contemporary community standards), (2) depicts or describes sexual conduct in a patently offensive way, and (3) lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miller v. California (1973) defines obscenity using local community standards for prurient appeal and patency offensiveness; typically applied to hard-core pornography. State statutes (e.g., anti-obscenity laws) have been upheld or struck down based on application of Miller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child pornography exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Child pornography is categorically unprotected (New York v. Ferber); restrictions do not depend on the Miller test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech or materials involving sexual exploitation of children may be regulated regardless of artistic or literary value; courts have allowed stricter regulation for child-protective reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incitement — imminent lawless action (Brandenburg test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that incites imminent lawless action is not protected; Brandenburg established the 'imminent lawless action' test, replacing the earlier 'clear and present danger' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Brandenburg v. Ohio, advocacy is unprotected only when directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action. This is a high bar for the government to satisfy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting words doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflammatory words that are either injurious by themselves or likely to cause the hearer to immediately retaliate (fighting words) are not necessarily protected under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates from Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire and subsequent cases; fighting-words restrictions are narrowly circumscribed because of risks to peaceful expression and public order. The doctrine interacts with 'heckler's veto' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: True threats doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: True threats are not protected speech (see Watts v. United States; Virginia v. Black).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats that a reasonable listener would interpret as a serious expression of intent to harm are unprotected. Courts evaluate context and speaker intent; recent cases refine mens rea required for criminal liability (e.g., Elonis, Counterman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech integral to criminal conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that is integral to criminal conduct (e.g., instructions to commit a crime) is not protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have allowed suppression when speech is directly tied to facilitating or committing unlawful acts. Case examples include New York v. Ferber and United States v. Hansen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial speech — intermediate scrutiny (Central Hudson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial speech (speech that 'propose[s] a commercial transaction') is not wholly outside First Amendment protection but is subject to intermediate scrutiny; Central Hudson established a four-part intermediate-scrutiny framework for commercial speech restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial-speech regulations must survive Central Hudson analysis (the page notes Central Hudson holds such restrictions are subject to a four-element intermediate scrutiny). Courts ask whether the speech is lawful and non-misleading, whether the government interest is substantial, whether the regulation directly advances that interest, and whether it is not more extensive than necessary. Cases: Ohralik, Central Hudson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation — actual malice for public-figure plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on libel and slander attach civil liability; New York Times Co. v. Sullivan established the 'actual malice' standard for public-figure plaintiffs, a high bar to recover for defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-figure plaintiffs must show the defendant knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth. Private-figure standards are lower. Defamation law balances reputation against free expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public employee speech — official duties vs citizen speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by public employees pursuant to their official duties are not protected by the First Amendment from employer discipline (Garcetti v. Ceballos); speech by public employees as citizens on matters of public concern may be protected under Pickering and Lane v. Franks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish between speech made as part of job duties (no protection) and speech as a private citizen (possible protection). Cases examine government interest in efficient public services and employees' interest in speaking on matters of public importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student speech — Tinker substantial interference and school exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Students enjoy First Amendment protection at public schools absent a showing of 'substantial interference with school discipline or the rights of others' (Tinker). However, subsequent cases (Bethel, Hazelwood, Morse) permit certain curricular, indecent, or school-supervised speech restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tinker protects student protests and symbolic speech unless disruptive. Bethel allows disciplinary action for indecent campaign speech; Hazelwood allows school administrators to restrict school-sponsored expression; Morse permits regulation of pro-illicit-drug messages at school events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive conduct / symbolic speech protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonverbal conduct intended to communicate a message (symbolic speech) is protected under the First Amendment, but protection can turn on context and intent (e.g., flag burning, silent marches, clothing, computer code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have applied full protection in many cases but sometimes apply intermediate scrutiny to content-neutral regulations. Examples: Texas v. Johnson (flag burning), Spence v. Washington; expressive conduct may be treated differently when mixed with non-speech elements (Kleinman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague and meaningless expression generally protected
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous or difficult-to-articulate expressions (instrumental music, abstract art, nonsense) are generally included in 'speech' and protected, though some justifications for protection may not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hurley v. Irish-American GLIB Group affirmed protection for Pollock's art, Schoenberg's music, and the poem Jabberwocky. Courts sometimes apply intermediate scrutiny when artistic expression mixes with non-speech elements (e.g., painted junked cars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled speech and compelled subsidy of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment protects against some forms of compelled speech and compelled financing of others' speech; the government generally cannot force individuals or corporations to speak or finance speech with which they disagree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases recognize limits on compelled speech (e.g., Barnette, Wooley) and address compelled subsidies or assessments (Janus, Abood line). The doctrine includes complex doctrine about compelled subsidy of others' speech and mandatory contributions to collective speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overbreadth and vagueness doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes that are overbroad (chill protected expression) or unconstitutionally vague may be struck down; courts use these doctrines to invalidate speech restrictions that sweep too widely or fail to give fair warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overbreadth allows invalidation of laws that restrict substantial protected speech relative to legitimate applications. Vagueness doctrine requires that regulated persons have reasonable clarity about prohibited conduct and prevents arbitrary enforcement.
